title: Think more rain means more river water? Not necessarily
summary:
Some rivers are receiving more rain than before but have lower water flow, according to a study

More rain and snow equals more water in rivers, right? Not necessarily. A new study shows that, despite receiving more rainfall than they used to, river water levels are falling because of changes in climate.

Global heating is intensifying the hydrological cycle, making wet regions wetter and dry regions drier, but how is this affecting river flow? Researchers from the Pennsylvania State University, in the US, have analysed precipitation and river flow records in more than 10,000 rivers between 1951 and 2020. In nearly one-third of rivers, they found that flow trends did not match with the changes observed in rainfall and snow.

Not necessarily Some rivers are receiving more rain than before but have lower water flow, according to a study Kate Ravilious Thu 1 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More rain and snow equals more water in rivers, right? Not necessarily. A new study shows that, despite receiving more rainfall than they used to, river water levels are falling because of changes in climate. Global heating is intensifying the hydrological cycle, making wet regions wetter and dry regions drier, but how is this affecting river flow? Researchers from the Pennsylvania State University, in the US, have analysed precipitation and river flow records in more than 10,000 rivers between 1951 and 2020. In nearly one-third of rivers, they found that flow trends did not match with the changes observed in rainfall and snow. The findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters , show that more than 10% of rivers receive more precipitation now than they did 50 years ago but have lower rates of flow. This mismatch appears to be more common in regions where rainfall extremes are becoming more common, and where evaporation rates are high. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. This research highlights the need to understand the other factors that control river flow, and monitor trends in river discharge rates, as well as precipitation, to predict future water availability in a changing climate.
